title: Three ideas called "agent"
scenario:
You lead operations at an online furniture shop with 40 staff. After a vendor demo, three teams each sent in an "agent" idea for next quarter. You have budget for one pilot.

The COO asks you which ideas really need an agent, which one to pilot, and what the pilot must include. The exhibit shows the three proposals.
exhibit:
Agent proposals: Q1 (made-up example data)

A. Product copy
   Task:   rewrite each new product description in French
   Steps:  always the same: read text -> translate -> save
   Volume: 60 products a week

B. Delivery complaints
   Task:   answer "where is my sofa?" messages; look up the order,
           check the carrier, offer a new date or a refund
   Steps:  differ per case (1 to 8 lookups)
   Success measure: complaint closed without a second contact
   Human review: team lead checks every refund

C. "Improve the business"
   Task:   read all company data each night and find ways to grow
   Steps:  open-ended
   Success measure: none yet
   Limits: none ("let it run until it is done")

questions.prompt: Using Anthropic's definitions, how should you describe proposal A?

options.text: An agent, because a model does the translation without a person writing each sentence by hand.
options.explanation: Using a model doesn't make it an agent. In Anthropic's post, an agent directs its own steps; here the steps never change.

options.text: A workflow at most: the path is fixed, so one prompt or a short fixed chain fits.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's post calls a fixed, predefined path a workflow and recommends the simplest solution that works.

options.text: An agent, because it runs every week without anyone starting it by hand, so it acts alone.
options.explanation: A schedule says when it runs, not who chooses the steps. The steps are still fixed.

options.text: A chatbot, because it talks to a customer and answers in their language.
options.explanation: A chatbot holds a conversation. Proposal A has no conversation: it translates text on a fixed path, which the post calls a workflow.

questions.prompt: Which proposal fits agent work best, based on Anthropic's post?

options.text: C, because it is the most open-ended, and agents are built for open-ended work.
options.explanation: Open-ended is only one part. The post also asks for clear success criteria and human oversight, and C has neither.

options.text: A, because it has the highest weekly volume, so the agent saves the most time.
options.explanation: Volume doesn't decide it. A has a fixed path, which the post calls a workflow.

options.text: A, because translating text is the most repeatable work, and repeatable work needs an agent most.
options.explanation: Repeatable work with a fixed path is what the post calls a workflow. Agents fit tasks where the steps can't be predicted in advance.

options.text: B: the steps vary per case, it mixes talk and action, success is clear, and a human checks refunds.
options.explanation: Right. The post says agents add most value for tasks with conversation and action, clear success criteria, feedback loops and human oversight. Support is its own example.

questions.prompt: The team behind C says: "No limits needed. It stops when it is done." What is the best reply?

options.text: Agree: limits would stop the agent before it finds its best ideas, and the report would be thinner.
options.explanation: Anthropic's Agent SDK docs warn that without limits the loop can run long on open-ended prompts.

options.text: Agree, as long as a manager reads the final report each morning.
options.explanation: Reading the report afterwards doesn't limit how long the loop runs or what it costs during the night.

options.text: Disagree: open loops can run long and cost a lot; set a turn limit and a budget.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's SDK docs call a budget a good default for production agents, and Google's overview says one interaction can use 100k to 3M tokens.

options.text: Disagree: agents always stop after ten steps, so it will never finish this task.
options.explanation: Speed is not the main risk here. Without a limit you set, the loop runs until the model finishes, which can take long and cost a lot.

questions.prompt: You pick B. Which risk from Anthropic's post should the pilot plan for most?

options.text: Compounding errors: one wrong lookup early can lead to a wrong offer at the end.
options.explanation: Right. The post says agents bring higher costs and the potential for compounding errors, and it recommends testing in sandboxed environments with guardrails.

options.text: That the agent will be too fast for customers, who expect slower replies.
options.explanation: The post doesn't name speed as a risk here. It names cost and compounding errors.

options.text: That the agent can't read order data, since agents only work with text.
options.explanation: The post says support agents can pull customer data and order history through tools.

options.text: Agents are slow, so the pilot should plan for long waits, not for wrong answers.
options.explanation: The refund check helps, but wrong dates or wrong order lookups would still reach customers. The post still recommends testing and guardrails.
